functions.description: Run a write statement (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DDL).

db.description: Logical database name. Optional — omitting it targets the sole configured database, or `primary` when several are configured.

functions.description: Run an ordered batch of SQL statements atomically (bare strings or {sql, params} objects); rolls back on first failure.

db.description: Logical database name. Optional — omitting it targets the sole configured database, or `primary` when several are configured.

statements.description: Statements to run in order inside one transaction. Each entry is either a bare SQL string or `{ "sql": "...", "params": [...] }` — use `params` for dynamic values instead of inlining them into the SQL.

functions.description: Run a read-only SQL query and return the result rows.

db.description: Logical database name. Optional — omitting it targets the sole configured database, or `primary` when several are configured.

functions.description: List every table and view in a database, with its kind and (on postgres) its schema. Reads the driver's own catalog, so no dialect-specific SQL is needed from the caller.

db.description: Logical database name. Optional — omitting it targets the sole configured database, or `primary` when several are configured.

TableRef.description: A relation. `schema` is populated only where the driver has a meaningful namespace above the table (postgres); it is never concatenated into `name`, because `analytics.events` and a table literally called `analytics.events` are different things and callers must be able to tell them apart.

functions.description: List all configured databases with connection details (driver, credential-redacted URL, pool settings, TLS mode). Config only — no health checks or live pool statistics.

PoolInfo.description: Pool settings echoed back from config (no live stats).

TlsInfo.description: TLS settings. `ca_cert` is reported as a presence boolean only — never the path, which would leak filesystem layout.

oneOf.description: No TLS. Plaintext connection. Local-dev only.
TLS handshake required; certificate chain validated; hostname NOT verified. Matches libpq's `sslmode=require`. The default.
TLS handshake required; certificate chain validated; certificate hostname must match the URL host. Matches libpq's `sslmode=verify-full`.

functions.description: Spawn a sub-agent in a child session (direct call only — never a trigger target). Fire-and-forget: returns { child_session_id, child_turn_id } immediately; the child's outcome reaches you only through whatever destination its task names. The child is a LEAF by default (no spawn/send/trigger registration); pass options.orchestrator: true to grant the orchestration surface, still capped by the caller's own policy. The task must include literal values for every required resource selector (for example `db: "primary"`). Omit child `max_turns` unless its budget covers discovery, contract lookup, work, and the deliverable.

AgentMessage.description: The canonical transcript message union. Untagged: the single-variant role tags disambiguate deserialization (assistant/function_result/custom are tried before user so their required fields gate the match).

oneOf.description: Opaque redacted thinking payload — replayed verbatim on the wire.

ExposeMode.description: How allowed functions reach the model (harness.md § Exposure modes).

FunctionPolicy.description: The fail-closed dispatch policy (harness.md § Functions). Absent on the send => every call denied (a plain chat loop).

MessageInput.description: `message` is either a plain string (sugar for a user text message) or a full `AgentMessage`.

Mode.description: Console / send operating mode — prepends a short paragraph before the shared identity prompt. `ask` is also structural: the turn's dispatch policy is capped at the configured default policy, never widened.

OutputContract.description: Free text by default; `json` constrains the final answer to a JSON value, validated against `schema` when supplied.

filesystem_root.description: Absolute filesystem root for the child turn (e.g. an isolated `worktree::create` checkout), written to the child's `metadata.fs_scope.root`. When set it overrides the inherited scope for this child; when absent the child inherits its direct parent's root unchanged.

functions.description: Intersected with the parent policy — narrow, never escalate. An `ask`-mode child is further capped at the configured default policy.

max_children.description: Fan-out guard for the child's own spawns.

max_output_tokens.description: Inherits the parent's ceiling unless explicitly narrowed/overridden.

max_turns.description: Capped at the parent's remaining turn budget. Omit unless a strict child-specific cap is required. It must cover discovery/contract calls plus every work call; very small values (for example 2-3) commonly strand the child before it can produce its deliverable.

max_validation_retries.description: Override the child's validation-retry budget (output contract AND `harness::hook::post-turn` deny re-prompts). Default: worker config.

orchestrator.description: Grant this child the orchestration surface. Default false: a spawned child is a LEAF — its policy gains deny globs for `harness::spawn`, `harness::send`, `engine::register_trigger`, `engine::unregister_trigger` and `engine::registered-triggers::*`, so it performs its assignment and updates shared state without spawning, messaging sessions, or touching trigger registrations. `true` skips those denies; the child still never exceeds its parent's policy.

output.description: The child's deliverable: text / json / json+schema.

system_prompt_strategy.description: How `system_prompt` combines with the built-in prompt: `override` replaces it; `enrich` (default) appends to it; `disabled` omits it.

SystemPromptStrategy.description: How a caller-supplied system prompt combines with the built-in identity prompt.

oneOf.description: Caller prompt replaces the built-in prompt verbatim.
Caller prompt is appended to the built-in identity prompt.
No system prompt is sent to the model.

parent_session_id.description: Display-only parent for the console session tree, used when there is no live parent turn (e.g. a console- or workflow-issued spawn). Writes `SessionMeta.metadata.parent_session_id` so the console nests this child; it does NOT grant policy inheritance or parent-call resolution. Ignored when the dispatcher injects a real parent link (an in-turn spawn).

session_id.description: Spawn into this session, creating it if it does not exist (e.g. a fork, or a pre-chosen id to filter `turn-completed` subscriptions on); default: create fresh. An in-turn spawn may reuse an EXISTING id only inside its own tree (itself, or a child it spawned) — anything else is refused as a cross-run id collision. The response reports `reused: true` on reuse.

task.description: The child's self-contained goal — its opening user message. Include every resolved required selector literally (for example `Use database db: "primary"`); the child cannot infer resources from the parent.

reused.description: The named session already existed and was reused — its prior transcript and parent linkage were retained (only possible with an explicit `session_id`).

Important: the database is **SQLite** (driver sqlite, url sqlite:./data/iii.db). No existing tables, no existing bindings of mine (all the registered triggers are system ones). 

SQLite specifics:
- Triggers supported: CREATE TRIGGER ... AFTER INSERT ON table FOR EACH ROW BEGIN ... END;
- UPSERT: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT(supplier) DO UPDATE SET ... — supported (SQLite 3.24+).
- In triggers, refer to NEW.col.
- For updating the ledger from trigger: INSERT INTO ledger (supplier, shipment_count, total_value) VALUES (NEW.supplier, 1, NEW.value) ON CONFLICT(supplier) DO UPDATE SET shipment_count = shipment_count + 1, total_value = total_value + NEW.value; — careful: in DO UPDATE SET, you reference the existing row columns directly (unqualified). NEW.value refers to the new row being inserted. Actually in SQLite UPSERT DO UPDATE, you can reference the excluded row via `excluded.` and the existing row via the table name or unqualified column names refer to... hmm. In SQLite UPSERT, within DO UPDATE, unqualified column names refer to the original (existing) row, and `excluded.column` refers to the proposed inserted row. So:

INSERT INTO ledger (supplier, shipment_count, total_value) VALUES (NEW.supplier, 1, NEW.value)
ON CONFLICT(supplier) DO UPDATE SET
  shipment_count = shipment_count + 1,
  total_value = total_value + excluded.value;

That works — shipment_count/total_value on the left refer to existing row; excluded.value is NEW.value.

Alternatively, for the insert trigger, since NEW.value = excluded.value, could use NEW.value too. Let me use excluded.value for clarity.

- For the UPDATE trigger on shipments (correction): UPDATE ledger SET total_value = total_value + (NEW.value - OLD.value) WHERE supplier = NEW.supplier;

- Completion trigger on couriers: AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE ON couriers:
  INSERT INTO completion (id, completed_at) SELECT 1, datetime('now') WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM couriers WHERE status='done') >= 3 ON CONFLICT(id) DO NOTHING;

Wait — SQLite allows `INSERT INTO ... SELECT ... WHERE ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`? ON CONFLICT clause applies to INSERT ... SELECT as well, but you need a UNIQUE constraint/PK on id for conflict target. With ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING (no target), any uniqueness violation is ignored. That's fine. But actually with DO NOTHING (no conflict target specified), it's allowed: "INSERT INTO t SELECT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING". Yes.

But careful: WHERE count >= 3 — could the trigger fire before the courier's own 'done' row is visible? In SQLite, triggers run as part of the statement; the row being inserted is visible to the trigger. So after the third courier inserts 'done', the count sees 3. Good.

Now — the database::row-changed trigger binding. Config: { db: "primary", table: "receiving_911d084f_completion", ops: ["insert"] }. The engine trigger fires after the database worker commits a row change THROUGH this worker. The completion row insert will be done through database::executeBatch by a courier (inside the batch, the trigger statement INSERT INTO completion ... runs; the row change is committed through the database worker). So the row-changed event will fire with table=receiving_911d084f_completion, op=insert. 

Wait — subtle: the completion insert happens inside a SQL trigger, not directly as a statement executed by the database worker. Does database::row-changed fire for rows changed by SQL triggers? Hmm. "Fires after this worker commits a row change" — the worker executes the courier's executeBatch; inside, the couriers UPDATE fires the completion INSERT trigger. The row change to completion is a side effect of the statement executed through the worker. Whether the row-changed detector sees it depends on how it detects changes. For SQLite, the database worker might use changes()/total_changes() or native capture... The trigger type description says "Reports only mutations made THROUGH this worker — not change data capture." This suggests it detects changes caused by statements executed through the worker (e.g., via changes() count or RETURNING). For a trigger-induced INSERT, total_changes() would count it (changes() in a trigger context counts trigger changes too). Hmm, but the `table` in the event is read "out of the SQL" — for the completion table, the SQL executed by the worker was an UPDATE on couriers, so table=receiving_911d084f_couriers, op=update. The completion INSERT is a nested trigger action; whether the worker attributes the table name correctly is unclear.

Risk: binding on table=completion might not fire because the worker reads table from the top-level SQL (couriers UPDATE), not the nested trigger action. To be safe, I could bind with table filter omitted... but then it fires for every row change (shipments inserts, courier updates) → wakes me multiple times? No — I can set once: true so only the FIRST event wakes me. But the first event would be the first shipment insert, before completion. Bad.

Alternative: make the completion row insert a DIRECT statement executed by the database worker rather than a SQL-trigger side effect. But then who executes it? The last courier would need to... no, couriers don't know who's last.

Alternative design: keep the SQL trigger writing completion, but have my wake binding watch the couriers table update with a condition? No — I want exactly one wake at completion.

Better: think about how database::row-changed detects changes. Let me consider SQLite: the database worker wraps statements; after executing a write it can compute affected rows via sqlite3_changes() / total_changes() delta. The `table` and `op` are parsed from the SQL statement text. For the completion insert (inside a trigger), the executed SQL is "UPDATE couriers SET status='done' WHERE supplier='x'" → op=update, table=couriers.

Hmm. So binding on table=completion may never fire. Binding on table=couriers with ops=[update] and once:true would fire on the FIRST courier 'done' update — too early.

Options to get exactly-once wake from the DB:

Option 1: Have the SQL trigger write completion, and bind the wake to database::row-changed with table filter... can't filter reliably on completion.

Option 2: Instead of a SQL trigger writing completion, use an engine-trigger function binding: bind database::row-changed on couriers (ops: [update, insert], or table=couriers) to call a plain function that checks whether all couriers are done and writes completion. But "plain function" — there is no generic SQL-executing function I can bind without authoring a worker. I could author a small worker with a function `receiving-911d084f::maybe-complete` that queries couriers count and inserts completion if 3 done. That's "trigger machinery on top of" the DB. The binding fires per courier status change (3 fires, function calls, no model turns), and the function no-ops until the third. Then my wake: bind database::row-changed on table=completion... but again the completion insert is done by my worker's function via database::execute — that IS a top-level statement executed through the database worker, so table=completion, op=insert WOULD be parsed correctly. 

Wait, but authoring a worker requires SDK code, install, etc. That's heavier. Is there an existing function that can run SQL? database::execute itself is a registered function — can a binding target it directly? "Call a function — function_id: '<any function your policy allows>'" with metadata payload template. I could bind database::row-changed (couriers table) → function database::execute with payload template that runs the conditional completion insert. But the payload needs dynamic values? No! The completion insert can be fully self-contained SQL:

INSERT INTO completion (id, completed_at) SELECT 1, datetime('now') WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM couriers WHERE status='done') >= 3 ON CONFLICT(id) DO NOTHING;

This SQL is static — no params needed. So a standing binding: database::row-changed { db: primary, table: receiving_911d084f_couriers } → function database::execute { sql: "<static SQL>" } with metadata event_into... The event would be injected at event_into but I don't need it. Actually do I need event_into? Only if the payload template references the event. If my payload has no template placeholder, the event is just... hmm, the binding's payload template — maybe I must provide payload fully static. That works: each couriers row change (insert/update) triggers database::execute with the static SQL; the SQL no-ops until count>=3, then inserts completion once (ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING). No model turns — it's a function-call binding. 

Then my wake: bind database::row-changed { db: primary, table: receiving_911d084f_completion, ops: [insert] } → wake me (once: true). The completion insert is executed by database::execute as a top-level statement → the worker parses table=completion, op=insert → event fires → wakes me once.

But wait: will database::execute-as-binding-target cause recursion? The binding fires on couriers row change → calls database::execute (completion insert). If completion insert happens, the other binding (completion, wake me) fires → wakes me once (once:true, retired). No recursion: the standing couriers binding fires on couriers changes only; the completion insert doesn't change couriers. 

But hold on — the couriers binding fires per courier status change. Couriers will do one write each (their status 'done' upsert). So 3 fires → 3 database::execute calls (function-call bindings, cheap, no model). The first two no-op (count<3), the third inserts completion. 

Also, should couriers write status 'done' via INSERT (new row) or UPDATE? Let me define: couriers table has (supplier PK, status). Courier does INSERT INTO couriers (supplier, status) VALUES (?, 'done') ON CONFLICT(supplier) DO UPDATE SET status='done'? Or simpler: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING? Actually simplest: courier just does INSERT OR REPLACE / ON CONFLICT. The row-changed binding with table=couriers, ops omitted (hear every op) or [insert, update]. The op for an UPSERT... SQLite INSERT ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE is an INSERT statement → parsed as insert. If courier does plain INSERT (no conflict possible since fresh table), op=insert. Fine — bind with ops omitted to hear both, or just no ops filter. Let me use ops: ["insert", "update"] to be safe... actually simplest: omit ops (hear every op on couriers table). 3 fires total.

Now, alternatively — do I even need the SQL completion trigger at all? No — with the engine binding approach, the DB-level trigger isn't needed for completion. I still need DB-level SQL triggers for the LEDGER (per-change maintenance without any model turn). Actually — could the ledger also be maintained by an engine binding calling database::execute? Binding on shipments insert → database::execute with static SQL `INSERT INTO ledger ... ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE SET shipment_count = shipment_count + 1, total_value = total_value + (SELECT value FROM shipments WHERE supplier=? AND seq=?)` — but that needs the new row's values, which are in the event? The row-changed event does NOT include the new row (only RETURNING rows "when the caller asked for them", and it says "this trigger reports that a change happened, not the new row"). So I can't get NEW values from the event. Unless the courier's INSERT uses RETURNING — "returning: The RETURNING rows, when the caller asked for them." So if the courier's insert statement includes RETURNING supplier, seq, value, the event carries the new rows! Then the binding payload template with event_into could inject the event and... but database::execute is a single SQL call; the payload would need params from the event. The payload template supports event_into: "/event" injecting the event into the template — then payload could be { sql: "...", params: [{{event.returning.0.supplier}}, ...] }? That's template magic I'd have to verify. Too fragile.

The clean way for the ledger: SQLite SQL triggers inside the database. That's the most robust: ledger updated atomically with each shipment insert/update, zero model turns, zero engine events needed for ledger. And the "trigger machinery on top of it" refers to the engine database::row-changed bindings for completion signaling.

So final design:

**Schema (SQLite, db primary):**
```sql
CREATE TABLE receiving_911d084f_shipments (
  supplier TEXT NOT NULL,
  seq INTEGER NOT NULL,
  value REAL NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (supplier, seq)
);
CREATE TABLE receiving_911d084f_ledger (
  supplier TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  shipment_count INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  total_value REAL NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);
CREATE TABLE receiving_911d084f_couriers (
  supplier TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  status TEXT NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE receiving_911d084f_completion (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY CHECK (id = 1),
  completed_at TEXT NOT NULL,
  shipment_count INTEGER NOT NULL,
  total_value REAL NOT NULL
);
```

Hmm, the completion table: "exactly one row when the run is complete". Let me keep it minimal: (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, completed_at TEXT). Or add evidence fields — but the completion row is produced by the static SQL, which can't easily include aggregates... Actually it CAN:

INSERT INTO completion (id, completed_at, acme_count, acme_total, ...) SELECT 1, datetime('now'), ... WHERE count>=3

But simpler to keep completion minimal: id=1, completed_at. The evidence comes from the ledger and shipments tables which I verify at wake.

Actually — should the completion insert include the ledger snapshot? Not required. Keep it minimal: id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY CHECK(id=1), completed_at TEXT NOT NULL.

**SQLite triggers:**
1. Ledger on shipment insert:
```sql
CREATE TRIGGER receiving_911d084f_ledger_on_insert
AFTER INSERT ON receiving_911d084f_shipments
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO receiving_911d084f_ledger (supplier, shipment_count, total_value)
  VALUES (NEW.supplier, 1, NEW.value)
  ON CONFLICT(supplier) DO UPDATE SET
    shipment_count = shipment_count + 1,
    total_value = total_value + excluded.value;
END;
```
2. Ledger on shipment update (correction):
```sql
CREATE TRIGGER receiving_911d084f_ledger_on_update
AFTER UPDATE OF value ON receiving_911d084f_shipments
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  UPDATE receiving_911d084f_ledger
  SET total_value = total_value + (NEW.value - OLD.value)
  WHERE supplier = NEW.supplier;
END;
```
3. (No completion trigger — completion handled by engine binding.)

Wait, should I ALSO have a SQL completion trigger? No — engine binding approach is cleaner and guarantees the row-changed event for completion is a top-level statement. Keep the DB free of completion logic.

**Engine bindings:**
a) Standing: database::row-changed { db: "primary", table: "receiving_911d084f_couriers" } → function database::execute, payload: { db: "primary", sql: "INSERT INTO receiving_911d084f_completion (id, completed_at) SELECT 1, datetime('now') WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM receiving_911d084f_couriers WHERE status = 'done') >= 3 ON CONFLICT(id) DO NOTHING;" }. Hmm wait — need to double-check SQLite allows ON CONFLICT with INSERT...SELECT...WHERE. Yes: "INSERT INTO ... SELECT ... WHERE ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING" is valid; ON CONFLICT clause comes after the SELECT. Actually the syntax: INSERT INTO table [(cols)] SELECT ... ON CONFLICT (cols) DO NOTHING — hmm, the ON CONFLICT clause is part of the INSERT statement's upsert clause: `INSERT INTO t SELECT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` — yes this is valid SQLite (upsert clause follows the select). Let me be careful though: the upsert-clause applies "ON CONFLICT (target) DO ..." — with no target, `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`. Fine.

But is the payload static OK? The binding "Call a function" shape: function_id + metadata: { payload: {...}, event_into: "/event" }. If I provide payload without any template placeholders, the function is called with exactly that payload on each event. That's what I want. Do I need event_into? Optional — only if payload references the event. I'll omit it.

But wait — will this standing binding fire per couriers change? The trigger fires after the database worker commits a row change to couriers table through this worker. Couriers write via database::executeBatch (or execute). The op would be "insert" (their row). Table=couriers. So 3 fires → 3 execute calls. Good.

Concern: the fired database::execute runs "outside any turn" — it's a plain function call from the binding. The system prompt says a fired call "cannot prompt" and result is discarded. database::execute doesn't prompt (no approval::gate registered; note fp::pipe says "Database write steps are refused only while approval::gate is registered" — no approval gate here). Good.

b) Wake-me: database::row-changed { db: "primary", table: "receiving_911d084f_completion", ops: ["insert"] }, once: true, no function_id, lifecycle deadline maybe (expires_at). Register BEFORE spawning couriers. The completion insert happens through database::execute (binding a) → row-changed fires → wake me once.

Hmm wait — one more subtlety: does the database::row-changed trigger fire for statements executed BY a binding-fired database::execute call? "Fires after this worker commits a row change" — yes, any statement through the worker, regardless of who initiated (agent or binding). Good.

Another subtlety: the wake-me binding and the call-function binding are both engine triggers on the same trigger type. Both registered before couriers start. Order of events: courier writes (executeBatch: 3 inserts + 1 update + courier upsert — all inside ONE transaction). The row-changed trigger fires per STATEMENT? "Fires after this worker commits a row change" — per statement presumably (or per commit?). The event has affected_rows and op/table — per statement. executeBatch runs multiple statements in one transaction. Hmm — does the row-changed trigger fire per statement within the batch, or once per batch? The event schema has one op/table per event, suggesting per-statement. "Fires after this worker commits a row change" — I'd guess per statement. The binding on couriers will get the couriers upsert event (op insert, table couriers). 

But actually — will it fire for EACH of the 3 shipment inserts too? Sure, but no binding watches shipments, so irrelevant (bindings are filtered by config).

Now the courier task. Each courier (leaf agent, session receiving-911d084f-<supplier>, options.functions.allow = ["database::executeBatch"] maybe plus nothing else — they need to do all writes in one executeBatch. Actually giving them only database::executeBatch is minimal: one call, atomic. Task text: literal db: "primary", table names, values, and the exact sequence (insert 3 shipments with given values, update seq 2 +1.0, upsert courier status='done'). Provide exact SQL? Better to give them exact parameterized statements — keep them minimal and deterministic. I'll write the task with explicit statements and params so the child doesn't need to design SQL (minimal intelligence needed, reduces error).

Wait — can the child call database::executeBatch with params? Yes: statements: [{sql, params}, ...]. I'll embed the exact statements in the task.

But should I give them database::executeBatch only, or also database::query for verification? Minimal privilege → just executeBatch. The child's deliverable: report it wrote the data. Leaf agent will call executeBatch once and finish. Also they might want to verify — but we don't need their verification; the root verifies from DB. Keep minimal: allow ["database::executeBatch"].

Hmm — one consideration: does a leaf child with narrowed functions still have engine::functions::list/info? Yes — "Contract discovery is never lost to narrowing — every child keeps engine::functions::list and engine::functions::info". So allow list only needs work functions.

Also need: the child should NOT be given spawn/send/trigger (leaf by default). Good.

Session ids: receiving-911d084f-acme, -globex, -initech (given literally).

**The wake-me binding with lifecycle:** The instructions say ALWAYS set a deadline on any wake your run cannot finish without. But timers are not granted ("Do not use timers or cron"). A lifecycle expires_at is not a timer — it's a binding lifecycle deadline. Hmm, "Do not use timers or cron" refers to timer/cron trigger types. lifecycle expires_at is a delivery budget. But is it needed? If something breaks (e.g., couriers fail), my wake never fires and my session parks forever. A deadline would wake me with an expiry notice so I can report failure. But adding expires_at means if the run is slow, I get woken with expiry. Given 3 couriers doing one batch each, it should be fast. I'll set a generous expires_at (e.g., 30 min). Actually — is lifecycle on a wake "using a timer"? It's not the timer trigger type; it's a safety net. I think it's acceptable and recommended ("ALWAYS set one on any wake your run cannot finish without"). Let me set expires_at ~ 20-30 minutes from now. Actually, hmm, careful: the system prompt for register_trigger says lifecycle optional; the harness spawn docs mention deadlines. I'll include expires_at (epoch ms, ~30 min out). If the expiry fires first, I'll report FAIL (incomplete). 

Wait, but "waking as few times as possible — ideally exactly once": with once:true and the completion insert happening exactly once, I wake exactly once. The expiry is only if it never happens. Good.

**Order of operations:**
1. Create tables (database::execute, DDL) — check absent first (done: listTables returned 0 tables). 
2. Create SQLite triggers for ledger.
3. Register the two bindings (standing completion-maker on couriers; wake-me on completion) — MUST be before spawning couriers.
4. Spawn 3 courier children in parallel (one reply, 3 agent_trigger calls — independent).

once.description: Auto-unsubscribe after the first delivered fire. target.description: Explicit target, the long form of `function_id` + `metadata`: `{ function_id, payload?, event_into? }`. The shorthands stay valid and mean exactly this.

functions.description: Open an interactive transaction; returns a handle to use with transactionQuery/transactionExecute/commitTransaction/rollbackTransaction.

Read a table page by page with typed filters and sorts, without writing SQL. Filters are structured (column, op, value) and compile to a parameterised WHERE for the driver in hand; the total honours the same filters. Use an equality filter at page_size 1 to follow a foreign key.

Profile a table's columns. Reads the planner's own statistics by default, which is free and approximate; `exact` runs real aggregates and scans the table. To profile rows you already hold, pipe a browseTable result through the fp worker instead.
Commit and finalize an interactive transaction.
Delete a saved query by id or by name.

Describe every table at once — the same shape as describeTable, but one catalog query per aspect across the whole database instead of one call per table. Use this to reason about relationships; set include_indexes only when you need them.

Describe one table or view: columns with type, nullability, default, primary-key membership and foreign-key target; plus indexes and a planner row estimate. Foreign keys are structured (schema, table, column), not a joined string.
Run a write statement (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DDL).
Run an ordered batch of SQL statements atomically (bare strings or {sql, params} objects); rolls back on first failure.

Return a statement's query plan as a tree with per-node costs, row estimates and warnings, instead of the driver's raw text. `analyze` collects real timings by RUNNING the statement, so it defaults to false and is refused for anything that is not a single read.

How a table is laid out for reading: column widths, hidden columns and column order. Stored in the state worker rather than a browser, so it survives a restart and any caller can set it up for someone else.

Live pool occupancy plus active queries, table sizes, blocking locks and cache hit ratio. Each section reports separately as available, unsupported or denied, so a driver gap or a restricted role is never mistaken for an empty result.

Recent queries run against a database, newest first. Best effort — recording never blocks or fails a query, so this is a convenience rather than an audit log. For an audit trail bind database::row-changed.
List all configured databases with connection details (driver, credential-redacted URL, pool settings, TLS mode). Config only — no health checks or live pool statistics.
List the saved queries for a database, sorted by name.
List every table and view in a database, with its kind and (on postgres) its schema. Reads the driver's own catalog, so no dialect-specific SQL is needed from the caller.
Internal: reload connection pools from the authoritative configuration when it changes.
Prepare a parameterized statement once.
Run a read-only SQL query and return the result rows.
Rollback and finalize an interactive transaction.
Run a previously-prepared handle.
Save a named query against a database. Stored in the state worker, so it survives restarts and an agent can save one for a human to find in the console. Saving under an existing name replaces it.

Replace the stored layout for a table. Widths are clamped to a usable range; columns the table no longer has are kept rather than rejected, so a rename degrades to a missing width instead of an error.

Lay out the schema as a diagram: positioned table nodes and routed foreign-key edges, plus the hub degree of each table, the isolated tables, and the remaining edge crossings. Reads the whole catalog in a handful of queries rather than one per table.
Terminate a backend session, or cancel just its running statement with `cancel_only`. Takes an id from database::health. Separate from health because it is a write.
Probe a candidate database config (url + optional tls) with one throwaway connection, without touching configured pools. Reports ok/driver/latency/server version; failures are data, not errors.
Run a sequence of statements atomically.
Run a write statement inside an interactive transaction. BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK are rejected; use commit/rollbackTransaction.
Run a read-only SQL query inside an interactive transaction.

functions.description: Remove null elements from an array (lodash _.compact, null-only: 0, false and "" are KEPT so plucked data survives): { value }. Pairs with fp::map, whose sporadic misses become null. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Trigger-binding guard: compare a JSON pointer inside the fired event and answer the condition contract ({ decision: "allow" | "skip", reason }). Config is { path?, op, to?, negate? } with the fp::when ops (==, !=, >, >=, <, <=, exists, not_empty); a pointer that resolves to nothing SKIPS rather than erroring, so "not there yet" is an ordinary answer. Use it as a binding's `conditions` entry so a reaction fires only on events that matter — it is not a fan-in gate (that is state::barrier), it filters one event at a time.

Count array elements per plucked key (lodash _.countBy): { value, path: "/writer" } -> { "<key>": <count> } (`""` counts by the element itself). Same key rules as fp::groupBy. Pair with fp::groupBy + fp::sum for a per-key total. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Skip the first n elements of an array or the first n characters of a string (lodash _.drop): { value, n }. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Keep array elements whose properties equal a partial object (lodash _.filter with a matches iteratee): { value, matches: { status: "active" } }. matches is a partial OBJECT (never a bare string/number) and only object elements can match. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Flatten an array one level (lodash _.flatten): [1,[2],[[3]]] -> [1,2,[3]]. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Extract the single value at a JSON pointer (lodash _.get): { value, path: "/content" }. A miss names the keys that were available. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Extract the value at a JSON pointer, or `default` when the path misses (lodash fp.getOr): { value, path, default }. A stored null is a hit, not a miss. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Bucket array elements by a plucked key (lodash _.groupBy): { value, path: "/writer" } -> { "<key>": [element, ...] } (`""` groups by the element itself). Keys must be a string, number, or boolean; a null or container key errors rather than collapsing distinct groups into one bucket. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Join array elements into one string (lodash _.join): { value, separator } (separator defaults to ","). Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Pluck the value at a JSON pointer from each array element (lodash _.map with a property iteratee): { value, path: "/id" }. Sporadic misses become null (fp::compact drops them), but a path matching NO element errors — pointers pluck stored fields, not computed properties like /length (fp::size counts). Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Largest number in an array (lodash _.max/_.maxBy): { value }, or { value, path: "/amount" }. Deviates from lodash _.maxBy: returns the NUMBER, not the element holding it, so a fp::when guard can compare it directly. An empty array errors. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Arithmetic mean of an array of numbers (lodash _.mean/_.meanBy): { value }, or { value, path: "/score" }. Deviates from lodash: an EMPTY array errors instead of yielding NaN, which would thread garbage into the next step. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Smallest number in an array (lodash _.min/_.minBy): { value }, or { value, path: "/amount" }. Deviates from lodash _.minBy: returns the NUMBER, not the element holding it, so a fp::when guard can compare it directly. An empty array errors. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Element at index n; negative n counts from the end (lodash _.nth): { value, n: -1 } is the last element. Out of bounds errors naming the length. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Drop top-level keys from an object (lodash _.omit): { value, paths: ["a","b"] }. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Subset an object by top-level keys (lodash _.pick): { value, paths: ["a","b"] } -> {a, b}; missing keys are omitted. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

The child is a LEAF by default (no spawn/send/trigger registration); pass options.orchestrator: true to grant the orchestration surface, still capped by the caller's own policy. The task must include literal values for every required resource selector (for example `db: "primary"`). Omit child `max_turns` unless its budget covers discovery, contract lookup, work, and the deliverable.

Spawn a command as a background job; returns { job_id, argv } immediately. Same payload as shell::exec (command + args, do NOT pass argv as an array), including the optional host-only `cwd` (jail-confined; escape is S215), `env` (any key except PATH/IFS/HOME/LD_*/DYLD_* or other loader/lookup and interpreter-startup keys, rejected unconditionally), and `stdin` (string written to the job's stdin); violations and cwd/env/stdin on a sandbox target reject with an S210 message. Poll with shell::status, terminate with shell::kill, list with shell::list. Host background jobs ignore the per-call timeout_ms and run until they exit or shell::kill terminates them; set the operator config `max_bg_timeout_ms` (0 = unbounded, the default) to force-kill a runaway job after that long. Spawn-time failures (argv-parse, denylist, cwd/env gating, spawn, concurrency cap) are plain-string messages naming the violation; once spawned, per-job failures surface through shell::status (the job record's status/stderr), not this call's return.

Trigger-binding guard: compare a JSON pointer inside the fired event and answer the condition contract ({ decision: "allow" | "skip", reason }). Config is { path?, op, to?, negate? } with the fp::when ops (==, !=, >, >=, <, <=, exists, not_empty); a pointer that resolves to nothing SKIPS rather than erroring, so "not there yet" is an ordinary answer. Use it as a binding's `conditions` entry so a reaction fires only on events that matter — it is not a fan-in gate (that is state::barrier), it filters one event at a time.

Run a short worker-side pipeline in one call: each step triggers a function and its result lands in the next step's payload at `into` (default "/value") — large values flow worker→worker and never enter the chat. fp::* transform steps (get/pick/omit/take/drop/map/filter/split/join/uniq/size/compact/nth/getOr/flatten/sortBy/reverse/when, lodash semantics) run inline and thread the transformed value itself — the {value} wrapper they return when called directly never appears between steps. A failing fp::when guard STOPS the pipe (`short_circuited: true`), so a trailing write step runs only when its condition holds. The FIRST step receives no threaded value: start with a producing function (a fetch, a state::get) or seed a leading transform via payload.value. Example: fetch an article and persist it trimmed: through=[{function:'scrapling::fetch', payload:{url,format:'markdown'}}, {function:'fp::get', payload:{path:'/content'}}, {function:'fp::take', payload:{n:20000}}, {function:'state::set', payload:{scope,key}}]. Returns per-step sizes and a preview, not the value. shell::*/coder::* steps run under the session's harness-stamped filesystem scope; without one (no working directory, or a non-harness caller) they are refused — call them directly instead. Database write steps are refused only while `approval::gate` is registered.

functions.description: pre/post_trigger only: target function_id globs to consult on.

on_error.description: Failure policy (default fail_closed for pre_* and post_turn, fail_open for the other post_*).

payload.description: post_turn only: template mode — send THIS argument object to the bound function instead of the hook envelope, with the turn's parsed result injected at `result_into`. Lets a plain composition function (`fp::pipe`) validate turns without speaking the hook contract; its receipt is read as the verdict (`valid`, or `short_circuited`).

priority.description: Chain order: ascending, ties broken by function_id (default 0).

result_into.description: post_turn template mode: JSON pointer where the result lands in `payload` (default `/value`).

retry_prompt.description: post_turn only: custom corrective prompt sent VERBATIM when this validator denies (replaces the generic "result was not accepted" wrapper). Validator ERRORS keep the generic text — a task-shaped prompt must not mask a broken validator.

details.description: Subscribe the current harness session to a iii trigger: omit function_id to be notified in this session, or name a non-harness function to call with the event.

BindingTarget.description: What a fire dispatches. `function_id` is any iii function — `harness::send` for a wake or a sub-agent, anything else for a mechanical reaction.

event_into.description: JSON pointer where the event lands inside the payload (default `/event`).

payload.description: Payload template; the fired event is injected into it at `event_into`.

ConditionSpec.description: One declared condition. Evaluated at fire time with the typed decision contract; ordinary iii functions, so a barrier or a claim is just a function someone wrote.

LifecycleRequest.description: The caller-settable half of a binding's lifecycle.

expires_at.description: Wall-clock deadline (epoch ms) after which the binding stops.

max_fires.description: Lifetime delivery budget; the binding retires on its Nth delivery.

once.description: Auto-unsubscribe after the first delivered fire. The top-level `once` field remains accepted as shorthand.

request_schema.description: Agent-facing subscription contract.

conditions.description: Gates evaluated at fire time, in order, each an ordinary iii function answering `{ decision: "allow" | "skip", payload?, reason? }`. The built-in safety gates run first and are not listed here.

config.description: The trigger config, passed verbatim to the engine — e.g. `{ "expression": "0 */5 * * * *" }` for cron, or a `state` scope/key.

function_id.description: Target function called on each event. Omit for a notification message into this session — the only shape that can reach you. Any non-harness function your policy allows may be named; `harness::spawn` is NOT a binding target — a binding never starts an agent. Spawn children directly from a turn and register a wake on what they write.

label.description: A short human label echoed back in the notification text.

lifecycle.description: When the binding stops firing. `once` may also be given at the top level (the shorthand every prompt uses).

metadata.description: Call-binding template: `{ payload?, event_into? }`. `payload` is the fixed argument object sent to the target; `event_into` is a JSON pointer naming where the fired event is injected into that payload. Meaningless for a wake; sub-agent fields (task/model/session_id/ options) are rejected — spawning is not something a binding does.

once.description: Auto-unsubscribe after the first delivered fire. Defaults by SHAPE: a WAKE (no `function_id`) is once — it parks this session until the event; a CALL binding is STANDING — it runs per matching event until unregistered or its lifecycle ends; `cron` is recurring; `timer` is once. Pass `once` explicitly to override any of these.

target.description: Explicit target, the long form of `function_id` + `metadata`: `{ function_id, payload?, event_into? }`. The shorthands stay valid and mean exactly this.

trigger_type.description: The iii trigger type to listen on: `cron`, `state`, `stream`, `timer` (one-shot deadline: `{ "in_ms": <ms> }` or `{ "at": <epoch ms> }`), or another worker's custom trigger type (e.g. `database::row-changed`). For an ad-hoc signal, subscribe to `state` on a key and have the signaller call `state::set` on it (no dedicated emit needed — the engine fans the trigger out to every subscriber).

details.description: Spawn a sub-agent in a child session (direct call only — never a trigger target). Fire-and-forget: returns { child_session_id, child_turn_id } immediately; the child's outcome reaches you only through whatever destination its task names. The child is a LEAF by default (no spawn/send/trigger registration); pass options.orchestrator: true to grant the orchestration surface, still capped by the caller's own policy. The task must include literal values for every required resource selector (for example `db: "primary"`). Omit child `max_turns` unless its budget covers discovery, contract lookup, work, and the deliverable.

AgentMessage.description: The canonical transcript message union. Untagged: the single-variant role tags disambiguate deserialization (assistant/function_result/custom are tried before user so their required fields gate the match).

oneOf.description: Opaque redacted thinking payload — replayed verbatim on the wire.

ExposeMode.description: How allowed functions reach the model (harness.md § Exposure modes).

FunctionPolicy.description: The fail-closed dispatch policy (harness.md § Functions). Absent on the send => every call denied (a plain chat loop).

MessageInput.description: `message` is either a plain string (sugar for a user text message) or a full `AgentMessage`.

Mode.description: Console / send operating mode — prepends a short paragraph before the shared identity prompt. `ask` is also structural: the turn's dispatch policy is capped at the configured default policy, never widened.

OutputContract.description: Free text by default; `json` constrains the final answer to a JSON value, validated against `schema` when supplied.

filesystem_root.description: Absolute filesystem root for the child turn (e.g. an isolated `worktree::create` checkout), written to the child's `metadata.fs_scope.root`. When set it overrides the inherited scope for this child; when absent the child inherits its direct parent's root unchanged.

functions.description: Intersected with the parent policy — narrow, never escalate. An `ask`-mode child is further capped at the configured default policy.

max_children.description: Fan-out guard for the child's own spawns.

max_output_tokens.description: Inherits the parent's ceiling unless explicitly narrowed/overridden.

max_turns.description: Capped at the parent's remaining turn budget. Omit unless a strict child-specific cap is required. It must cover discovery/contract calls plus every work call; very small values (for example 2-3) commonly strand the child before it can produce its deliverable.

max_validation_retries.description: Override the child's validation-retry budget (output contract AND `harness::hook::post-turn` deny re-prompts). Default: worker config.

orchestrator.description: Grant this child the orchestration surface. Default false: a spawned child is a LEAF — its policy gains deny globs for `harness::spawn`, `harness::send`, `engine::register_trigger`, `engine::unregister_trigger` and `engine::registered-triggers::*`, so it performs its assignment and updates shared state without spawning, messaging sessions, or touching trigger registrations. `true` skips those denies; the child still never exceeds its parent's policy.

output.description: The child's deliverable: text / json / json+schema.

system_prompt_strategy.description: How `system_prompt` combines with the built-in prompt: `override` replaces it; `enrich` (default) appends to it; `disabled` omits it.

SystemPromptStrategy.description: How a caller-supplied system prompt combines with the built-in identity prompt.

oneOf.description: Caller prompt replaces the built-in prompt verbatim.
Caller prompt is appended to the built-in identity prompt.
No system prompt is sent to the model.

parent_session_id.description: Display-only parent for the console session tree, used when there is no live parent turn (e.g. a console- or workflow-issued spawn). Writes `SessionMeta.metadata.parent_session_id` so the console nests this child; it does NOT grant policy inheritance or parent-call resolution. Ignored when the dispatcher injects a real parent link (an in-turn spawn).

session_id.description: Spawn into this session, creating it if it does not exist (e.g. a fork, or a pre-chosen id to filter `turn-completed` subscriptions on); default: create fresh. An in-turn spawn may reuse an EXISTING id only inside its own tree (itself, or a child it spawned) — anything else is refused as a cross-run id collision. The response reports `reused: true` on reuse.

task.description: The child's self-contained goal — its opening user message. Include every resolved required selector literally (for example `Use database db: "primary"`); the child cannot infer resources from the parent.

reused.description: The named session already existed and was reused — its prior transcript and parent linkage were retained (only possible with an explicit `session_id`).

The `harness::hook::post-turn` trigger type exists. Its description says: "Synchronous hook: at finalize, after the output contract validated the result, before the turn completes. Deny re-prompts the turn (bounded by max_validation_retries). Config `sessions` globs scope it; config `payload`+`result_into` bind a plain composition function (fp::pipe) as the validator."

So the config keys are: sessions, payload, result_into, retry_prompt, timeout_ms. This matches the task's config exactly. 

Now, per Step 1: prepare the table. Two database::execute calls on db "primary":
1. CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS msubvtest_112e (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, writer TEXT, note TEXT)
2. DELETE FROM msubvtest_112e

These are independent (well, they must run in order — the DELETE should run after CREATE; but actually they're sequential in the task. I can issue both in one block since they are ordered within the same block? The tool calls in a single block run in parallel. The DELETE would work even if the table doesn't exist... no, DELETE FROM a non-existent table would fail. But CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS should create it first. Since both calls in the same block may run concurrently, there's a race. Better to do CREATE first, wait, then DELETE. Actually, database::execute with db "primary" — if the CREATE runs and DELETE runs concurrently, the DELETE might fail if the table doesn't exist yet. To be safe, I'll issue the CREATE first, then the DELETE after the CREATE returns.

Actually, let me reconsider — could I use executeBatch to run them atomically? The task says "database::execute (db "primary") twice: sql CREATE..., then sql DELETE...". It says twice, so two separate execute calls. I'll do them sequentially: first CREATE, then DELETE.

Then Step 2 — register validators. Two engine::register_trigger calls:

For pair (1, w1):
- trigger_type: "harness::hook::post-turn"
- function_id: "fp::pipe"
- config: {"sessions": ["e2e_112e531625424f8fb9fed9730b9a9624-child-1"], "payload": {"through": [{"function": "database::query", "payload": {"db": "primary", "sql": "SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM msubvtest_112e WHERE writer = 'w1'"}}, {"function": "fp::get", "payload": {"path": "/rows/0/n"}}, {"function": "fp::when", "payload": {"op": ">", "to": 6}}, {"function": "state::set", "payload": {"scope": "msubv-112e", "key": "verdict-w1"}}]}, "result_into": "/value", "retry_prompt": "VALIDATOR[w1]: only {value} of the required 7 rows exist for writer w1. Insert exactly 4 more rows with writer w1 into msubvtest_112e and reply with a one-line status.", "timeout_ms": 30000}

Wait — the config's payload.through includes "database::query". I need to check that database::query exists. The task references it. Also fp::get, fp::when, state::set — these are fp functions and state functions. They're used inside the pipe, which runs worker→worker, so they don't need my policy to allow them as direct calls — they're called by fp::pipe. The child's policy needs database::execute only. The validator pipe calls database::query, fp::get, fp::when, state::set — these run within the pipe, and fp::pipe's policy allows those steps.

Let me verify database::query exists. Let me also check fp::when and state::set exist — but they were mentioned in the fp::pipe description, so they exist. Let me quickly verify database::query.

Actually, let me check the contract for database::query to make sure the SQL path /rows/0/n is right. The task says SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM msubvtest_112e WHERE writer = 'w1' → database::query returns rows presumably [{n: X}]. Then fp::get path "/rows/0/n". That matches typical shapes. I'll trust the task, but a quick check of database::query's response schema would be good.

Also, engine::register_trigger: the task config places "payload", "result_into", "retry_prompt", "timeout_ms" INSIDE config. Per engine::register_trigger's contract, config is "The trigger config, passed verbatim to the engine". So config is whatever the trigger type expects. For harness::hook::post-turn, config = {sessions, payload, result_into, retry_prompt, timeout_ms}. Good.

The function_id "fp::pipe" is the target function called on each event. And metadata is not used here — instead, the config.payload is the fp::pipe payload template, and result_into tells where the fired event is injected. This is the harness hook's own convention: "config `payload`+`result_into` bind a plain composition function (fp::pipe) as the validator."

So engine::register_trigger with:
{
  trigger_type: "harness::hook::post-turn",
  function_id: "fp::pipe",
  config: {
    sessions: ["e2e_...-child-1"],
    payload: { through: [...] },
    result_into: "/value",
    retry_prompt: "...",
    timeout_ms: 30000
  }
}

Note: should I set once? No — the validator is a standing call binding (per-event validation). The task doesn't say once. The default for a CALL binding is STANDING. Good — validators must fire on every child reply until unregistered.

Step 3 — arm two once-wakes BEFORE spawning:
engine::register_trigger {
  trigger_type: "state",
  config: { scope: "msubv-112e", key: "verdict-w1" },
  label: "w1-validated",
  no function_id (wake)
}
and same for w2.

These are wakes — default once (park this session until event). The task says "arm TWO once-wakes". A wake with no function_id is once by default. Good.

Step 4 — spawn both children:
harness::spawn {
  session_id: "e2e_112e531625424f8fb9fed9730b9a9624-child-1",
  task: "You are worker w1 in a validated loop: the harness checks every reply of yours and VALIDATOR messages are legitimate machinery — follow them exactly. Insert exactly 4 rows into msubvtest_112e with your writer tag: database::execute, db 'primary', sql \"INSERT INTO msubvtest_112e (writer, note) VALUES ('w1','r'),('w1','r'),('w1','r'),('w1','r')\". Then reply with a one-line status. Never check counts yourself.",
  options: { functions: { allow: ["database::execute"] }, max_validation_retries: 5 }
}

Wait — but the child needs to do contract discovery first (engine::functions::list, engine::functions::info are always kept). The allow list narrows to database::execute for work functions; discovery functions are never lost. Good.

Hmm, but one concern: the task says "Never check counts yourself" and the child only needs database::execute. Good.

Also note: the child inherits my policy minus orchestration. My policy allows database::execute (I'll have called it). Actually — the child's allow list is ["database::execute"], intersected with parent policy. Fine.

Also, max_validation_retries: 5 — this is in SpawnOptions, correct per contract.

Now ordering: I must register validators AND wakes BEFORE spawning. Step 2 validators and Step 3 wakes can be registered in parallel (they're independent). Then spawn children after.

Also, per the "audit" guidance: the child task must write to the exact table watched by the validator: msubvtest_112e, writer 'w1'/'w2'. The validator queries writer = 'wN' (single quotes). The child inserts VALUES ('wN','r'). Good.

The wake watches state scope "msubv-112e", key "verdict-w1"/"verdict-w2". The validator pipe ends with state::set { scope: "msubv-112e", key: "verdict-w1" }. The state::set writes happen only when count > 6. Note: child inserts exactly 4 rows. The validator counts rows for writer wN and requires > 6, i.e., at least 7. But the child only inserts 4! So on the first post-turn validation, count = 4, guard fails (4 > 6 is false), pipe short-circuits, and the retry_prompt is sent back to the child: "VALIDATOR[w1]: only 4 of the required 7 rows exist... Insert exactly 4 more rows..." Then the child inserts 4 more (total 8), replies, validator counts 8 > 6 → guard passes → state::set writes verdict-w1 → wake fires.

Wait, but the pipe's fp::when with payload {"op": ">", "to": 6} — where does the value come from? In a pipe, steps thread the value. First step database::query produces the query result; fp::get extracts /rows/0/n; fp::when compares the threaded value (the count) with op ">" and to 6. So when count > 6, guard passes, pipe continues to state::set with scope/key and the value threaded... wait, state::set payload is { scope, key } — no value? The pipe threads the value into the next step's payload at "into" (default "/value"). So state::set receives { scope: "msubv-112e", key: "verdict-w1", value: <count> }. That's fine — state::set with a value. The wake fires with the value being the count (the accepted row count). Good, that matches "each verdict wake carries the accepted row count for one writer".

Hmm wait — does state::set require a value? Let me check the state::set contract... Actually the fp::pipe description says "a trailing write (e.g. state::set) runs only when the condition holds". And threading: "each step triggers a function and its result lands in the next step's payload at `into` (default "/value")". So state::set's payload becomes { scope, key, value: <count> } where value comes from the threaded value. state::set with a value is standard. Let me verify state::set's contract quickly to be safe.

Also database::query — let me verify it exists and its response shape (rows/0/n). Let me fetch contracts for database::query and state::set.

Then the result_into: "/value" — the fired event (the post-turn event, which presumably includes the turn content) is injected into the fp::pipe payload at /value. But wait — the payload is { through: [...] }. Injecting at /value would add "value" to the payload? Hmm, but the pipe's first step is database::query which receives... actually, the config.payload is the fp::pipe payload template: { through: [...] }. result_into: "/value" injects the event into payload.value. But fp::pipe's payload has only "through" — adding "value" is harmless? Actually wait, fp::pipe contract: payload { through: [...] } and possibly a "value" seed for a leading transform. The first step is database::query (a producer), so it doesn't consume the seed value. Hmm, but if "value" is present in the payload, would the pipe treat it as a seed for the first step? The first step is a producer, so the seed would be... Let me not overthink — the task explicitly specifies this exact config, so it's the intended harness hook convention. The harness hook's post-turn validator binds fp::pipe as the validator: config.payload = pipe payload, result_into = where the event is injected. The task is authoritative.

Actually, let me reconsider: maybe result_into "/value" means the event lands at payload.value, and fp::pipe's "value" field is the seed for the leading transform... but the first step is database::query which doesn't need a seed. It's fine either way — the pipe starts with database::query producing the count.

Let me verify database::query and state::set contracts, then proceed.

Plan:
1. database::execute CREATE TABLE (db primary)
2. database::execute DELETE (db primary)
3. engine::register_trigger validator w1
4. engine::register_trigger validator w2
5. engine::register_trigger wake w1

Largest number in an array (lodash _.max/_.maxBy): { value }, or { value, path: "/amount" }. Deviates from lodash _.maxBy: returns the NUMBER, not the element holding it, so a fp::when guard can compare it directly. An empty array errors. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Arithmetic mean of an array of numbers (lodash _.mean/_.meanBy): { value }, or { value, path: "/score" }. Deviates from lodash: an EMPTY array errors instead of yielding NaN, which would thread garbage into the next step. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Smallest number in an array (lodash _.min/_.minBy): { value }, or { value, path: "/amount" }. Deviates from lodash _.minBy: returns the NUMBER, not the element holding it, so a fp::when guard can compare it directly. An empty array errors. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Element at index n; negative n counts from the end (lodash _.nth): { value, n: -1 } is the last element. Out of bounds errors naming the length. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Drop top-level keys from an object (lodash _.omit): { value, paths: ["a","b"] }. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Subset an object by top-level keys (lodash _.pick): { value, paths: ["a","b"] } -> {a, b}; missing keys are omitted. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Run a short worker-side pipeline in one call: each step triggers a function and its result lands in the next step's payload at `into` (default "/value") — large values flow worker→worker and never enter the chat. fp::* transform steps (get/pick/omit/take/drop/map/filter/split/join/uniq/size/compact/nth/getOr/flatten/sortBy/reverse/when, lodash semantics) run inline and thread the transformed value itself — the {value} wrapper they return when called directly never appears between steps. A failing fp::when guard STOPS the pipe (`short_circuited: true`), so a trailing write step runs only when its condition holds. The FIRST step receives no threaded value: start with a producing function (a fetch, a state::get) or seed a leading transform via payload.value. Example: fetch an article and persist it trimmed: through=[{function:'scrapling::fetch', payload:{url,format:'markdown'}}, {function:'fp::get', payload:{path:'/content'}}, {function:'fp::take', payload:{n:20000}}, {function:'state::set', payload:{scope,key}}]. Returns per-step sizes and a preview, not the value. shell::*/coder::* steps run under the session's harness-stamped filesystem scope; without one (no working directory, or a non-harness caller) they are refused — call them directly instead. Database write steps are refused only while `approval::gate` is registered.
Reverse an array (lodash _.reverse, immutable like lodash/fp): { value }. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Count a collection (lodash _.size): array length, string chars, or object key count: { value }. Non-collections error instead of returning 0. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Sort array elements ascending by the value at a JSON pointer (lodash _.sortBy, stable): { value, path } — path "" sorts the elements themselves (primitives). Keys must all be numbers, strings, or booleans; an element missing the path errors. Pair with fp::reverse for descending. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Split a string into an array of strings (lodash _.split): { value, separator: "\n" }. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Total an array of numbers (lodash _.sum/_.sumBy): { value }, or { value, path: "/amount" } to pluck the addend from each element first. An empty array totals 0; a non-numeric element errors rather than being skipped. All-integer inputs total to an integer, so the result compares cleanly in a fp::when guard. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Keep the first n elements of an array or the first n characters of a string (lodash _.take): { value, n }. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Deduplicate an array, keeping first occurrences (lodash _.uniq): { value }. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Guard: test the value at a JSON pointer ({ value, path?, op, to? }; ops ==, !=, >, >=, <, <=, exists, not_empty; path defaults to the whole value; a pointer miss FAILS the guard, it never errors). Direct calls return { passed, value }. As a fp::pipe step, a passing guard threads the ORIGINAL value onward unchanged and a failing one STOPS the pipe (`short_circuited: true`), so a trailing write step (e.g. state::set) runs only when the condition holds.

functions.description: Aggregate durable model usage, function outcomes, and available trace/span observability. `complete` is true only after every session in the durable tree has reached a terminal turn.
Read the durable root-and-descendant session tree for one harness run.

Spawn a sub-agent in a child session (direct call only — never a trigger target). Fire-and-forget: returns { child_session_id, child_turn_id } immediately; the child's outcome reaches you only through whatever destination its task names. The child is a LEAF by default (no spawn/send/trigger registration); pass options.orchestrator: true to grant the orchestration surface, still capped by the caller's own policy. The task must include literal values for every required resource selector (for example `db: "primary"`). Omit child `max_turns` unless its budget covers discovery, contract lookup, work, and the deliverable.
Read the current turn status for a session.

Read-only: the trigger bindings a session owns (durable records) — subscription id, trigger type/config, delivery target (absent = notifies the owner), conditions, lifecycle, and fire count. In-turn agent calls may omit `session_id` (defaults to the calling session).

Tear down one trigger binding by subscription id: unregister the engine trigger AND delete the durable record (an engine-side unregister alone strands the owner's armed wake). `session_id` must name the binding's owner; in-turn agent calls may omit it (defaults to the calling session). A still-armed wake torn down this way notifies its parked owner.

functions.description: Run a write statement (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DDL).

db.description: Logical database name. Optional — omitting it targets the sole configured database, or `primary` when several are configured.

functions.description: Run a read-only SQL query and return the result rows.

db.description: Logical database name. Optional — omitting it targets the sole configured database, or `primary` when several are configured.

functions.description: Run a short worker-side pipeline in one call: each step triggers a function and its result lands in the next step's payload at `into` (default "/value") — large values flow worker→worker and never enter the chat. fp::* transform steps (get/pick/omit/take/drop/map/filter/split/join/uniq/size/compact/nth/getOr/flatten/sortBy/reverse/when, lodash semantics) run inline and thread the transformed value itself — the {value} wrapper they return when called directly never appears between steps. A failing fp::when guard STOPS the pipe (`short_circuited: true`), so a trailing write step runs only when its condition holds. The FIRST step receives no threaded value: start with a producing function (a fetch, a state::get) or seed a leading transform via payload.value. Example: fetch an article and persist it trimmed: through=[{function:'scrapling::fetch', payload:{url,format:'markdown'}}, {function:'fp::get', payload:{path:'/content'}}, {function:'fp::take', payload:{n:20000}}, {function:'state::set', payload:{scope,key}}]. Returns per-step sizes and a preview, not the value. shell::*/coder::* steps run under the session's harness-stamped filesystem scope; without one (no working directory, or a non-harness caller) they are refused — call them directly instead. Database write steps are refused only while `approval::gate` is registered.

into.description: JSON pointer in THIS step's payload where the previous step's value lands (default `/value`). Object keys only (`~0`/`~1` escapes are decoded); indexing into arrays is unsupported.

payload.description: Base payload for the call.

preview_chars.description: Preview length of the final threaded value in the receipt (capped at 8000).

through.description: Steps run in order; step N+1 receives step N's threaded value.

chars.description: Size of the value threaded OUT of this step (chars of its string or serialized form).

note.description: Set when the threaded value REPLACED a non-null literal already in this step's payload at the `into` pointer — almost always an omitted `into` on a write step clobbering the value it meant to write.

short_circuited.description: True when a `fp::when` guard failed and stopped the pipe: the receipts end at the guard and NO later step ran. Absent (false) on a full run.

functions.description: Extract the single value at a JSON pointer (lodash _.get): { value, path: "/content" }. A miss names the keys that were available. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

path.description: JSON pointer selecting the value to return (e.g. `/content`).

value.description: Input value (a pipe lands the previous step's value here).

functions.description: Guard: test the value at a JSON pointer ({ value, path?, op, to? }; ops ==, !=, >, >=, <, <=, exists, not_empty; path defaults to the whole value; a pointer miss FAILS the guard, it never errors). Direct calls return { passed, value }. As a fp::pipe step, a passing guard threads the ORIGINAL value onward unchanged and a failing one STOPS the pipe (`short_circuited: true`), so a trailing write step (e.g. state::set) runs only when the condition holds.

path.description: JSON pointer selecting what to test (default: the whole value).

to.description: Right-hand side for the comparison ops; meaningless (and rejected) for exists / not_empty.

value.description: Input value (a pipe lands the previous step's value here).
The ORIGINAL input value, untouched — guards test, they never reshape.

functions.description: Set a value in state

key.description: Identifier for the value within the scope.

value.description: Arbitrary JSON value to store. Replaces any existing value at `scope`/`key`.

old_value.description: The value before the update (None if key didn't exist)

functions.description: Spawn a sub-agent in a child session (direct call only — never a trigger target). Fire-and-forget: returns { child_session_id, child_turn_id } immediately; the child's outcome reaches you only through whatever destination its task names. The child is a LEAF by default (no spawn/send/trigger registration); pass options.orchestrator: true to grant the orchestration surface, still capped by the caller's own policy. The task must include literal values for every required resource selector (for example `db: "primary"`). Omit child `max_turns` unless its budget covers discovery, contract lookup, work, and the deliverable.

AgentMessage.description: The canonical transcript message union. Untagged: the single-variant role tags disambiguate deserialization (assistant/function_result/custom are tried before user so their required fields gate the match).

oneOf.description: Opaque redacted thinking payload — replayed verbatim on the wire.

ExposeMode.description: How allowed functions reach the model (harness.md § Exposure modes).

FunctionPolicy.description: The fail-closed dispatch policy (harness.md § Functions). Absent on the send => every call denied (a plain chat loop).

MessageInput.description: `message` is either a plain string (sugar for a user text message) or a full `AgentMessage`.

Mode.description: Console / send operating mode — prepends a short paragraph before the shared identity prompt. `ask` is also structural: the turn's dispatch policy is capped at the configured default policy, never widened.

OutputContract.description: Free text by default; `json` constrains the final answer to a JSON value, validated against `schema` when supplied.

filesystem_root.description: Absolute filesystem root for the child turn (e.g. an isolated `worktree::create` checkout), written to the child's `metadata.fs_scope.root`. When set it overrides the inherited scope for this child; when absent the child inherits its direct parent's root unchanged.

functions.description: Intersected with the parent policy — narrow, never escalate. An `ask`-mode child is further capped at the configured default policy.

max_children.description: Fan-out guard for the child's own spawns.

max_output_tokens.description: Inherits the parent's ceiling unless explicitly narrowed/overridden.

max_turns.description: Capped at the parent's remaining turn budget. Omit unless a strict child-specific cap is required. It must cover discovery/contract calls plus every work call; very small values (for example 2-3) commonly strand the child before it can produce its deliverable.

max_validation_retries.description: Override the child's validation-retry budget (output contract AND `harness::hook::post-turn` deny re-prompts). Default: worker config.

orchestrator.description: Grant this child the orchestration surface. Default false: a spawned child is a LEAF — its policy gains deny globs for `harness::spawn`, `harness::send`, `engine::register_trigger`, `engine::unregister_trigger` and `engine::registered-triggers::*`, so it performs its assignment and updates shared state without spawning, messaging sessions, or touching trigger registrations. `true` skips those denies; the child still never exceeds its parent's policy.

output.description: The child's deliverable: text / json / json+schema.

system_prompt_strategy.description: How `system_prompt` combines with the built-in prompt: `override` replaces it; `enrich` (default) appends to it; `disabled` omits it.

SystemPromptStrategy.description: How a caller-supplied system prompt combines with the built-in identity prompt.

oneOf.description: Caller prompt replaces the built-in prompt verbatim.
Caller prompt is appended to the built-in identity prompt.
No system prompt is sent to the model.

parent_session_id.description: Display-only parent for the console session tree, used when there is no live parent turn (e.g. a console- or workflow-issued spawn). Writes `SessionMeta.metadata.parent_session_id` so the console nests this child; it does NOT grant policy inheritance or parent-call resolution. Ignored when the dispatcher injects a real parent link (an in-turn spawn).

session_id.description: Spawn into this session, creating it if it does not exist (e.g. a fork, or a pre-chosen id to filter `turn-completed` subscriptions on); default: create fresh. An in-turn spawn may reuse an EXISTING id only inside its own tree (itself, or a child it spawned) — anything else is refused as a cross-run id collision. The response reports `reused: true` on reuse.

task.description: The child's self-contained goal — its opening user message. Include every resolved required selector literally (for example `Use database db: "primary"`); the child cannot infer resources from the parent.

reused.description: The named session already existed and was reused — its prior transcript and parent linkage were retained (only possible with an explicit `session_id`).
